EvoSpec: Evolving Speculative Decoding via
Real-Time Vocabulary and Parameter Adaptation

Shuyu Zhang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Lingfeng Pan Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Qicheng Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Yaqi Shi Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Yueyang Tan Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Ruyu Yan Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Jiaqi Chen Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Lixing Du Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China    Lu Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China Correspondence to: wanglu@xidian.edu.cn
Abstract

Speculative decoding accelerates Large Language Model inference via a draft-then-verify paradigm, yet the output projection layer becomes a bottleneck as vocabulary sizes scale. While existing static pruning methods effectively reduce this overhead, they suffer from precipitous drops in acceptance rate in specialized domains or topic-switching scenarios due to their inability to capture dynamic distribution shifts. To address this, we introduce EvoSpec, a framework that enables real-time evolution of the draft model through dynamic vocabulary and parameter adaptation. Unlike static or purely retrieval-based approaches, EvoSpec employs a context-aware mechanism that retrieves critical long-tail tokens via efficient semantic and statistical indexing. Furthermore, we propose a lightweight online alignment strategy utilizing curriculum learning to continually minimize the distributional gap between the draft and target models. Extensive evaluations across specialized domains (coding, law, and medicine) confirm that EvoSpec overcomes the limitations of static baselines. On EAGLE-3, it achieves a 1.13x speedup in these settings over the state-of-the-art static baseline FR-Spec, with 27% lower memory overhead than standard online adaptation.

Keywords: 
Speculative Decoding, Large Language Models, Efficient Inference, Online Learning, Test-Time Adaptation, Dynamic Vocabulary Adaptation

1 Introduction

While the autoregressive generation paradigm empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust generative capabilities, the prohibitive computational costs result in significant inference latency (Kim et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2024). Speculative Decoding (SD), operating on a draft-verify paradigm, has emerged as a key technique to mitigate this bottleneck (Leviathan et al., 2023). However, as the vocabulary size of modern LLMs surges, the efficiency bottleneck of draft models has shifted (Goel et al., 2025). Recent research indicates that in lightweight draft models, the projection computation overshadows the compact backbone, accounting for nearly 50%-60% of the generation time (Zhao et al., 2025b). Consequently, reducing the computational overhead caused by large vocabularies while maintaining a high acceptance rate has become a core challenge for further enhancing inference speed (Cai et al., 2025).

To alleviate the computational bottleneck, recent works have explored static vocabulary pruning strategies. By leveraging offline corpus statistics, these methods restrict the search space to a global high-frequency subset, significantly reducing FLOPs (Zhao et al., 2025b; Goel et al., 2025). However, such strategies lack robustness in maintaining acceptance rates, particularly in scenarios involving multi-turn dialogues with frequent topic switching, or in vertical specialized domains such as medicine and coding (Deng et al., 2025). Static tables fail to cover dynamically changing long-tail terms, leading to the omission of critical domain vocabulary (Zhao et al., 2025a). Furthermore, even within the covered vocabulary, static draft models suffer from a distribution shift relative to the target model (Zhou et al., 2023). Due to the inability to perceive the specific inference context, draft models struggle to accurately fit the target model’s probability distribution in specific local contexts (Ganesan et al., 2025).

To address the aforementioned distribution shift, some current works attempt to introduce online adaptation mechanisms, utilizing feedback from the large model to fine-tune the draft model in real-time during inference (Hong et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). However, these methods typically rely on expensive full-parameter updates or complex knowledge distillation objectives, incurring significant computational and memory overheads (Liu et al., 2023). Therefore, achieving dynamic vocabulary recall and efficient distribution alignment while minimizing overhead remains an urgent problem to be solved.

To systematically address large-vocabulary bottlenecks, we propose EvoSpec, a framework formulating SD as a dynamic optimization problem. Unlike paradigms relying on static statistics, EvoSpec empowers draft models with Test-Time Adaptation (TTA). Inspired by recommendation systems, we design a context-aware subspace retrieval mechanism to overcome the poor long-tail coverage of static tables. By leveraging lightweight vector indexing, this mechanism constrains the search space to a context-relevant semantic subset, ensuring precise domain term coverage with negligible latency. Furthermore, to handle non-stationary shifts, we introduce a curriculum-based online alignment strategy. This employs a self-paced objective to correct prediction biases in real-time, maintaining distributional consistency with the target model.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Dynamic Vocabulary Adaptation: Inspired by recommendation systems, we reframe vocabulary selection as a context-aware retrieval problem. Our mechanism captures long-tail semantics with negligible setup cost, overcoming the intrinsic limitations of static pruning where efficiency compromises coverage.

  • •

    Resource-Efficient Test-Time Alignment: We propose a closed-loop framework that treats speculative decoding as continuous adaptation. By employing curriculum-driven LoRA, we bridge the distributional gap on-the-fly with 27% lower memory overhead than full-parameter methods.

  • •

    Robust Acceleration in Specialized Domains: Extensive evaluations confirm an average speedup of 1.13×\times. EvoSpec effectively mitigates the primary projection bottleneck in lightweight models, demonstrating superior stability over static baselines in dynamic topic-switching scenarios.

2 Related Work

The autoregressive nature of LLM generation results in memory-bound latency, where inference speed is constrained by memory bandwidth rather than compute power (Xia et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024). SD addresses this by verifying multiple low-cost draft tokens within a single parallel forward pass of the target model (Zhou et al., 2024). Early SD methods relied on independent draft models, which are typically smaller versions of the target (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). However, the efficiency of these methods is often constrained by the significant computational and memory overhead required to maintain a separate model architecture, limiting the net acceleration gain in practical settings (Zhang et al., 2024). To mitigate this, state-of-the-art approaches have shifted toward feature-level fusion. Medusa  (Cai et al., 2024) augments the target model with multiple decoding heads by utilizing the target’s own high-level representations to predict future tokens. EAGLE series (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025b) further advance this by introducing a lightweight autoregressive head operating on the target’s feature space. Despite reducing draft generation costs, these methods still necessitate a computationally expensive projection over the full vocabulary at the draft head’s final layer, which persists as a major latency source (Cheng et al., 2024).

This vocabulary bottleneck becomes particularly acute as LLMs expand to support multilingual and code generation capabilities, causing vocabulary sizes to surge. Recent analyses, such as FR-Spec (Zhao et al., 2025b) and VocabTrim (Goel et al., 2025), identify the LM Head projection cost as a primary bottleneck for lightweight draft models, accounting for up to 60% of the draft generation time. Existing solutions primarily employ static vocabulary pruning, constructing a context-independent subset of global high-frequency tokens to reduce the search space. However, such methods rely on the assumption of static word frequencies and fail to capture long-tail tokens that become locally probable in specialized domains or during topic shifts (Holtzman et al., 2019). Consequently, static pruning leads to frequent Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) errors and precipitous drops in acceptance rates (Khandelwal et al., 2019). Beyond static pruning, CORAL (Xie et al., 2024) improves draft-side efficiency through order-agnostic iterative refinement and LM-head routing, but it does not explicitly construct a context-specific active vocabulary or perform online draft-target alignment under domain shifts. EvoSpec instead targets the vocabulary bottleneck directly by leveraging HNSW-based approximate nearest neighbor search on the LM Head weight matrix (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018).

Beyond architectural and vocabulary constraints, a critical limitation of standard SD is the distribution shift between the pre-trained draft model and the specific input distribution encountered during inference (Sun et al., 2024). Static draft models often perform poorly when processing user-specific prompts or novel topics. Online Speculative Decoding (OSD) (Liu et al., 2023) addresses this by treating verification signals from the target model as supervision to fine-tune the draft model via real-time distillation. Similarly, Test-Time Training paradigms update model parameters on test data to minimize prediction entropy or perplexity (Sun et al., 2020). However, naive full-parameter updates are computationally expensive and prone to instability. Integrating these insights, EvoSpec employs a lightweight Online LoRA mechanism (Hu et al., 2022). This approach is distinct from the update strategies in OSD and allows for robust handling of specialized distributions, overcoming the limitations found in prior static or purely retrieval-based approaches.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate the problem within the general context of SD. Given a target model ℳp\mathcal{M}_{p} and a draft model ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q}, the objective is to maximize the effective generation speedup. Let x<tx_{<t} denote the input context at step tt. The draft model generates a sequence of tokens which are verified by ℳp\mathcal{M}_{p} based on the rejection sampling criterion α\alpha (Leviathan et al., 2023).

While various SD architectures exist, Feature-Level SD currently represents the state-of-the-art (Li et al., 2024a). However, these methods share a critical computational bottleneck with standard approaches: the output projection. For any draft model, predicting the next token requires projecting the hidden state ht∈ℝdh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} onto the full vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} via the language model head WL​M∈ℝ|𝒱|×dW_{LM}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}:

pℳq​(x|x<t)=Softmax​(ht​WL​MT).p_{\mathcal{M}_{q}}(x|x_{<t})=\text{Softmax}(h_{t}W_{LM}^{T}). (1)

The complexity 𝒪⁡(d×|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(d\times|\mathcal{V}|), where dd is the hidden dimension, becomes prohibitive when |𝒱|>100​k|\mathcal{V}|>100k. Although our implementation primarily builds upon the EAGLE-3 architecture due to its superior baseline performance, this vocabulary bottleneck is intrinsic to the SD paradigm itself (Zhao et al., 2025b).

We formulate the acceleration of large-vocabulary models as a dynamic resource allocation problem. Our objective at each inference step tt is to construct a minimal local vocabulary subspace 𝒱t⊂𝒱\mathcal{V}_{t}\subset\mathcal{V} and adapt the draft parameters θt\theta_{t} to minimize computational overhead while satisfying a probabilistic coverage constraint. Formally, we aim to solve:

min𝒱t,θt|𝒱t|s.t.∑x∈𝒱tpℳp​(x|x<t)≥1−ϵ,\min_{\mathcal{V}_{t},\theta_{t}}\quad|\mathcal{V}_{t}|\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}p_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}(x|x_{<t})\geq 1-\epsilon, (2)

where ϵ\epsilon is a tolerance threshold for probability mass loss. Since the true target distribution pℳpp_{\mathcal{M}_{p}} is unavailable during the drafting phase, EvoSpec approximates this optimization via two coupled mechanisms: (1) a retrieval-based subspace construction to approximate the high-probability set of pℳpp_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}, and (2) test-time parameter adaptation to minimize the distributional divergence DK​L(pℳp||pℳq)D_{KL}(p_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}||p_{\mathcal{M}_{q}}) on the selected subspace 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}.

3.2 System Architecture

To approximate the optimization solution defined in Eq. (2) under real-time constraints, EvoSpec establishes a closed-loop feedback system as illustrated in Figure 1. The core philosophy is to decouple the intractable joint optimization into two asynchronous processes triggered by the target model’s output token status relative to the current reduced vocabulary.

  • •

    Path A: Vocabulary Expansion. When the verified token xtx_{t} falls outside the current subspace 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, it violates the coverage constraint. The system activates the dynamic vocabulary generator to recall missing terms. To mitigate the retrieval latency of Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW), this module operates asynchronously on the CPU. This design allows the retrieval process to overlap with the GPU-bound decoding phase, incurring no additional latency on the critical execution path (as empirically verified in Appendix C)

  • •

    Path B: Parameter Alignment. When xtx_{t} resides within 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, the sample becomes eligible for online alignment rather than being updated unconditionally. The alignment controller selectively inserts qualified samples into the replay buffer under its gating policy, and then applies a confidence-aware curriculum to dynamically weight them, so that LoRA updates can reduce distributional divergence while preserving training stability.

This bifurcated architecture allows EvoSpec to dynamically expand the search space 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and adapt parameters θt\theta_{t} simultaneously, effectively evolving the draft model to fit the target distribution on-the-fly without interrupting the inference pipeline. The complete inference procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1 (see Appendix A.1).

3.3 Dynamic Search Space Reduction

To address the optimization objective defined in Eq. (2), EvoSpec abandons the rigid full vocabulary in favor of a dynamic construction strategy. We approximate the optimal high-probability set by decomposing the search space into global and local components. At each inference step tt, the active vocabulary subspace 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} is formulated as the union of a static core and context-dependent dynamic subsets:

𝒱t=𝒱s​t​a​t​i​c∪𝒮s​e​m​(ht)∪𝒮g​r​a​p​h​(𝒮s​e​m),\mathcal{V}_{t}=\mathcal{V}_{static}\cup\mathcal{S}_{sem}(h_{t})\cup\mathcal{S}_{graph}(\mathcal{S}_{sem}), (3)

where 𝒱s​t​a​t​i​c\mathcal{V}_{static} denotes the top-KK frequent tokens representing the stationary distribution of general syntax. We establish 𝒮s​e​m\mathcal{S}_{sem} and 𝒮g​r​a​p​h\mathcal{S}_{graph} through embedding-based indexing and graph-based expansion, as described below:

Semantic Approximation via HNSW.

The projection pℳq​(x)p_{\mathcal{M}_{q}}(x) constitutes a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem. To bypass 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|) exhaustive search, we index the output embeddings WL​MW_{LM} using HNSW with norm augmentation (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018). Upon OOV detection, the hidden state hth_{t} queries this index to retrieve the top-NN nearest neighbors 𝒮s​e​m​(ht)\mathcal{S}_{sem}(h_{t}). This approximates the target distribution’s high-probability region with 𝒪⁡(log⁡|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(\log|\mathcal{V}|) complexity, efficiently capturing topic-specific terms missed by static tables.

Statistical Expansion via Sparse Graph.

Since semantic similarity often overlooks rigid sequential patterns, we incorporate statistical dependencies via a token co-occurrence graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}). Constructed from the SlimPajama corpus(Soboleva et al., 2023), the graph is pruned by a threshold τ\tau to ensure sparsity. We query 𝒢\mathcal{G} to identify high-probability successors for tokens in 𝒮s​e​m\mathcal{S}_{sem}. The resulting set 𝒮g​r​a​p​h\mathcal{S}_{graph} complements semantic retrieval by capturing fixed collocations and terminological constraints.

Subspace Maintenance under Budget Constraints.

To prevent unbounded expansion and enforce a fixed budget |𝒱t|≤Nb​u​d​g​e​t|\mathcal{V}_{t}|\leq N_{budget}, we employ an Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) policy. ARC dynamically balances recency and frequency to manage token eviction. This ensures 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} evolves to retain only the most context-relevant tokens, thereby stabilizing inference latency. Please refer to Appendix E for a qualitative analysis of this process.

3.4 Test-Time Adaptation via Online Alignment

While the dynamic vocabulary addresses the recall bottleneck, the static parameters θf​i​x​e​d\theta_{fixed} of the draft model inevitably suffer from distributional shift when facing unseen topics. To mitigate this, we introduce a lightweight online alignment strategy. Instead of indiscriminate updates, we propose a confidence-aware curriculum to stabilize the adaptation process.

Adaptive Horizon Weighting.

SD inherently involves hierarchical uncertainty: the first token prediction (k=1k=1) serves as the anchor, while subsequent predictions (k>1k>1) are subject to error accumulation. Naively optimizing all steps with equal weight introduces significant gradient noise from distal, low-confidence tokens. To address this, we construct a dynamic weighting curriculum using the cross-entropy loss of the first step, ℒb​a​s​e\mathcal{L}_{base}, as a real-time proxy for alignment confidence. The loss weight wkw_{k} for the kk-th speculative step is formulated as:

wk=exp(−β⋅ℒb​a​s​e⋅(k−1)),w_{k}=\exp\left(-\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{base}\cdot(k-1)\right), (4)

where β\beta is a sensitivity coefficient controlling the decay rate (see Appendix D for ablations). This mechanism establishes an auto-evolving curriculum. Under high uncertainty (large ℒb​a​s​e\mathcal{L}_{base}), wkw_{k} decays rapidly to filter out noisy long-range gradients, effectively reducing the objective to Next-Token Prediction. Conversely, under low uncertainty (small ℒb​a​s​e\mathcal{L}_{base}), the weight decay flattens as the draft model aligns with the context, automatically expanding the effective horizon to capture longer-range dependencies.

Online Parameter Update.

To enable efficient adaptation, we employ LoRA by freezing the pre-trained draft backbone θf​i​x​e​d\theta_{fixed} and only optimizing the rank-decomposition matrices Δ​θ\Delta\theta injected into the query and value projections (Wq,WvW_{q},W_{v}). Instead of standard cross-entropy, we implement distribution-level knowledge distillation. We maintain a buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} storing verified trajectories and their corresponding top-kk logits zz from the target model. These are converted into a soft target distribution p^ℳp\hat{p}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}} via temperature scaling (TT). The optimization objective minimizes the weighted KL divergence over the speculation horizon γ\gamma:

minΔ​θ𝒥=∑(x,z)∈ℬ∑k=1γwk⋅T2⋅DK​L(p^ℳp∥pℳqτ),\min_{\Delta\theta}\mathcal{J}=\sum_{(x,z)\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{k=1}^{\gamma}w_{k}\cdot T^{2}\cdot D_{KL}\left(\hat{p}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\parallel p_{\mathcal{M}_{q}}^{\tau}\right), (5)

where p^ℳp=Softmax​(zℳp(t​o​p​-​k)/T)\hat{p}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}=\text{Softmax}(z_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}^{(top\text{-}k)}/T) and pℳqτp_{\mathcal{M}_{q}}^{\tau} are the temperature-scaled distributions. This aligns the draft’s probability landscape with the target’s while avoiding the high memory overhead of storing full vocab logits.

4 Empirical Evaluation

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate EvoSpec across a spectrum of semantic stability:

  • •

    General Benchmarks: We utilize Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024), which aggregates standard datasets including WMT14 (MT, RU-EN) (Bojar et al., 2014), MT-Bench (Conversation) (Zheng et al., 2023), Natural Questions (RAG/QA) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), GSM8K (Math) (Cobbe et al., 2021), and CNN/DM (Summarization) (Nallapati et al., 2016). We select 80 test samples per task with a unified max length of 1024.

  • •

    Specialized & Dynamic Domains: To verify robustness, we incorporate HumanEval (Code) (Chen, 2021), Pile of Law (Legal) (Henderson et al., 2022), and PubMedQA (Medical) (Jin et al., 2019). Furthermore, we construct a synthetic Topic-Switching dataset by concatenating code and legal texts to simulate abrupt user intent shifts.

Models. We employ Qwen3-4B (Team, 2025) as the target model. Given that the computational overhead of output projection scales linearly with the vocabulary size |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| rather than the parameter count, this model serves as a valid proxy for investigating large-vocabulary bottlenecks, as it shares an identical vocabulary structure with its 70B+ counterpart. For draft models, we evaluate configurations based on the EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025b) architecture and Qwen3-1.7B.

Baselines. We compare EvoSpec against four distinct categories of methods: (1) Standard SD: We include EAGLE-3, the state-of-the-art feature-level SD, alongside Vanilla Autoregressive Decoding. (2) Static Pruning: We select FR-Spec, which employs static top-kk pruning derived from Slimpajama corpus statistics (Soboleva et al., 2023). (3) Alternative Acceleration Baseline: We include CORAL (Xie et al., 2024), which improves draft-side efficiency through order-agnostic iterative refinement and LM-head routing, representing a strong alternative to vocabulary-centric acceleration. (4) Online Adaptation: We use OSD (Liu et al., 2023), a dynamic method that performs online SD via full-parameter updates.

Implementation Details. Evaluation metrics include Mean Acceptance Length (MAL), End-to-End Speedup, and Peak GPU Memory Usage. We unify the speculation horizon to 6 for all methods (corresponding to the draft length γ\gamma for vanilla SD and tree depth for EAGLE-3). For tree-based models, we further cap the total token budget at 60. To balance efficiency and stability, the Online Alignment Controller operates asynchronously using an experience replay buffer with a capacity of B=32B=32. All experiments are conducted on a server equipped with dual NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs (24GB). Detailed hyperparameter configurations are provided in Appendix A.2 and Table 5.

4.2 Draft Quality and Inference Speedup

We investigate the performance of EvoSpec, implemented on the EAGLE-3 architecture, across two dimensions: the restoration of draft model capabilities on general benchmarks, and the translation of these capabilities into end-to-end speedups in specialized domains.

Validating the Necessity of Dynamic Expansion.

First, we verify whether our dynamic vocabulary mechanism effectively mitigates the performance degradation caused by static pruning. Table 1 details the MAL across six tasks in Spec-Bench.

The static baseline FR-Spec, constrained by its fixed 32k vocabulary, exhibits a clear regression in draft quality compared to the Full Vocab baseline, with the average MAL dropping from 3.78 to 3.54. The introduction of the dynamic mechanism significantly narrows this gap. By maintaining a dynamic buffer of just 1024 tokens, EvoSpec recovers the Average MAL to 3.65, effectively reclaiming 96.6% of the theoretical upper bound. This empirically demonstrates that the dynamic retrieval module successfully recalls semantic tokens missed by the static table, thereby repairing the knowledge collapse inherent in static pruning methods. To directly validate this coverage-based intuition, Appendix F reports the covered probability mass of the active vocabulary and Recall@256 against the target model’s top-kk tokens.

Speedup and Hyperparameter Trade-off.

While recovering MAL is essential, the ultimate goal is wall-clock acceleration. We evaluate the end-to-end speedup in vertical domains (Code, Law, Medicine), where static vocabularies typically face severe OOV challenges. As shown in Table 2, we compare EvoSpec against various configurations, including the strong baseline CORAL, to benchmark our vocabulary-centric approach against recent draft-side acceleration methods.

The static method FR-Spec (Static 32k) fails to achieve tangible speedups (1.00×1.00\times) because the latency reduction in projection is strictly negated by the drop in acceptance rate. In contrast, CORAL already provides a strong improvement over the static baseline (Speedup 1.10×1.10\times), confirming that improving draft consistency and draft-head efficiency is beneficial. EvoSpec further improves on this result by jointly recovering long-tail tokens and adapting the draft model online:

  • •

    Impact of Static Base: An overly aggressive static base (8k) leads to speed regression (0.96×0.96\times) even with dynamic expansion. This indicates that a minimal level of static linguistic competence is a prerequisite.

  • •

    Optimal Configuration: The Static 32k + Dyna 256 configuration achieves the optimal balance, delivering a consistent 1.13×\times speedup. It outperforms CORAL by combining dynamic vocabulary evolution with lightweight online alignment, which is particularly beneficial under domain-specific long-tail vocabulary and local distribution shift.

It is worth noting that while a 1.13×\times speedup might appear modest, the projection layer accounts for approximately 60% of the total latency in these settings. Consequently, EvoSpec yields substantial gains by mitigating this dominant bottleneck, effectively transforming the prohibitive vocabulary projection into a manageable amortized overhead. Based on these findings, we adopt Static 32k + Dynamic 256 as the default setting.

4.3 Adaptation to Dynamic Distribution Shifts

A core contribution of EvoSpec is the Online Alignment Controller, which enables the EAGLE-3 based draft model to evolve continuously. To visualize its efficacy, we track the MAL over a request sequence containing an abrupt topic switch.

Simulating Abrupt Shifts.

To simulate a drastic shift in user intent, we construct a synthetic Topic-Switching test stream. As illustrated in Figure 2, the stream begins with HumanEval to establish a technical context. At Request #100, the stream instantaneously transitions to Pile of Law or PubMedQA. This setup creates a cold start scenario for the target domain, rigorously testing the model’s ability to recall new vocabulary and align distributions in real-time.

Trajectory Analysis.

Figure 2 compares the adaptation trajectories of the Static Baseline (FR-Spec) and EvoSpec on the EAGLE-3 architecture. We observe two distinct phases: (1) Transient Misalignment: At the shift point (Request #100), EvoSpec (Red) exhibits a slight, temporary fluctuation. This occurs because the online parameters, previously tuned for the source domain, are initially misaligned with the incoming target distribution. (2) Adaptive Gain vs. Stagnation: The divergence becomes evident immediately after the shift. The Static Baseline (Gray) remains stagnant, fluctuating around a suboptimal plateau as its fixed vocabulary limits its ceiling. In contrast, EvoSpec rapidly adjusts its parameters, showing a clear upward trend. Within approximately 20 requests, it not only stabilizes but surpasses the static baseline. This empirically validates the effectiveness of our Adaptive Horizon Weighting (Eq. 4) in facilitating rapid distribution alignment. To complement this controlled switching analysis with a more realistic long-horizon setting, we further evaluate EvoSpec on 144 real multi-turn trajectories from LMSYS-Chat-1M in Appendix G, where EvoSpec remains superior in both acceptance length and end-to-end throughput.

4.4 Ablation Study

To dissect the specific contributions of the Dynamic Vocabulary Retrieval and Online Alignment Controller within the EAGLE-3 architecture, we conduct a comprehensive ablation study across nine diverse tasks. As illustrated in Figure 3, we establish the Static Base (FR-Spec) as the baseline and evaluate three variants:

  • •

    Static + CL-LoRA: Integrating the Online Alignment Controller into the static base, where Curriculum Learning is applied to update LoRA parameters (Eq. 4).

  • •

    Dynamic Vocab Only: Enabling dynamic vocabulary expansion but keeping parameters fixed.

  • •

    EvoSpec (Full): The complete framework combining both modules.

Recall is Prerequisite to Alignment in Vertical Domains.

In specialized domains (Pile of Law, PubMedQA, HumanEval), we observe that the Dynamic Vocab Only configuration yields substantial gains, significantly outperforming the Static + CL-LoRA baseline. For instance, in PubMedQA, simply retrieving domain terms boosts throughput far more than parameter tuning alone. This empirically proves that vocabulary insufficiency is the primary bottleneck in vertical scenarios. Without the physical presence of domain-specific tokens in the projection layer, aligning probabilities (θ\theta) via CL-LoRA is futile.

Lightweight Alignment Suffices for General Tasks.

Conversely, in general tasks (Conv, QA), the gap between Dynamic Vocab Only and the Static Base narrows. Here, the gain primarily stems from the alignment mechanism. Notably, our lightweight Static + CL-LoRA achieves performance comparable to the heavy Static + OSD. This indicates that calibrating the draft distribution to local shifts does not require expensive full-rank updates; our Curriculum Learning-based LoRA (CL-LoRA), which prioritizes short-term tokens for rapid adaptation, is sufficient and computationally more efficient.

Synergistic Optimality.

Finally, EvoSpec Full establishes the optimal performance envelope across all tasks. This confirms that dynamic recall and online alignment are orthogonal and complementary: the former solves the Out-Of-Vocabulary problem, while the latter addresses the Distribution Shift problem. Their integration enables EvoSpec to achieve robust acceleration regardless of domain specificity.

4.5 Resource Efficiency Analysis

A critical constraint for online SD is the GPU memory overhead incurred by real-time parameter updates. Standard methods like OSD require maintaining full optimizer states for the entire draft model, specifically the momentum and variance estimates in Adam. This substantial overhead can easily exceed hardware limits during inference.

To quantify the efficiency of our approach, we monitor the Peak GPU Memory Usage of the EAGLE-3 draft model across three representative specialized domains. To isolate the cost of the alignment module from vocabulary pruning, we conduct this comparison under a Full Vocabulary configuration, benchmarking EvoSpec (CL-LoRA) against OSD (Full Parameter Update).

Results. As reported in Table 3, EvoSpec demonstrates superior resource efficiency. While OSD consumes over 12GB of memory due to the storage of dense optimizer states, EvoSpec restricts updates to low-rank matrices, thereby reducing the memory footprint by approximately 27%. This significant reduction in memory overhead is decisive for deployment, making advanced online learning frameworks feasible even on consumer-grade hardware such as the NVIDIA RTX 4090.

4.6 Generalization Across Architectures

To demonstrate that EvoSpec functions as an architecture-agnostic module independent of specific frameworks like EAGLE, we verify its effectiveness within the standard Independent Draft-Verification paradigm. Unlike the feature-level integration in EAGLE, this classic setup employs a decoupled architecture where the draft model (Qwen3-1.7B) and target model (Qwen3-4B) operate separately. We evaluate the performance across specialized domains under varying vocabulary configurations.

Results and Analysis. As detailed in Table 4, the results confirm the high compatibility and universality of our approach:

  • •

    Universal Effectiveness in Decoupled Settings: In this standard decoupled architecture, the static baseline (FR-Spec) yields only marginal improvements (1.02×1.02\times). In contrast, EvoSpec (Static 32k + Dyna 256) successfully overcomes this limitation, achieving a robust 1.07×\times speedup. This demonstrates that dynamically recalling long-tail tokens offers a universal acceleration mechanism applicable to generic draft-verification loops, extending beyond specific feature-level optimizations like those in EAGLE.

  • •

    Architectural Independence of Dynamic Gains: Crucially, we observe that EvoSpec with a reduced 16k static base (1.05×1.05\times) outperforms the optimal static baseline with a 32k vocabulary. This recurrence of the pattern where a small dynamic vocabulary outperforms a large static one confirms that the advantage of dynamic retrieval is an intrinsic property of the vocabulary distribution, independent of the underlying model architecture. To further validate the universality of EvoSpec, we provide additional evaluation results on the Llama-3.2 (Dubey et al., 2024) model family in Appendix B.

5 Limitations

Our work has two primary constraints. First, our evaluation focuses on 3B/4B models. However, it is worth noting that SD naturally employs lightweight draft models even for massive targets (e.g., 70B+). Since the projection bottleneck is intrinsic to these compact drafters regardless of target scale, EvoSpec remains theoretically applicable to larger settings. Second, the efficiency of our dynamic vocabulary relies on asynchronous CPU masking. On resource-constrained edge devices with limited compute or shared memory bandwidth, the retrieval overhead may become non-negligible, suggesting a potential avenue for future GPU-resident indexing.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we addressed the critical bottleneck of static vocabulary pruning in SD, particularly within specialized domains. We introduced EvoSpec, a framework enabling real-time draft evolution via context-aware retrieval and curriculum-based alignment. Extensive evaluations confirm that EvoSpec overcomes the accuracy limitations of static baselines, achieving a 1.13×\times speedup over FR-Spec on EAGLE-3 while reducing memory overhead by 27% compared to standard online methods. Furthermore, our results verify that these benefits are architecture-agnostic. By enabling continuous evolution during inference, EvoSpec offers a robust solution for efficient large-vocabulary model deployment.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning, specifically by improving the inference efficiency of Large Language Models. By reducing memory footprint and computational overhead, our research aims to lower the hardware barriers for deploying advanced models, potentially contributing to the democratization of AI technology and improved energy efficiency. We do not believe our work introduces new specific ethical or societal concerns beyond those inherent to the underlying models being accelerated.

Appendix A Implementation Details & Pseudocode

A.1 Algorithm Pseudocode

Algorithm 1 outlines the inference process of EvoSpec. The core innovation lies in the asynchronous execution of vocabulary expansion (CPU) and the event-triggered online alignment (GPU), which ensures that the main decoding pipeline remains non-blocking.

A.2 Hyperparameter Settings

Table 5 details the specific hyperparameter configurations used in our main experiments. These settings are shared across all datasets unless otherwise specified.

A.3 Additional Runtime Details

Beyond the global hyperparameters summarized in Table 5, we provide several implementation details omitted from the main paper for space reasons.

HNSW semantic retrieval.

We build the HNSW index offline over the target model’s LM-head output embeddings, where each token corresponds to one row of the output projection matrix. We apply the standard norm-augmentation trick so that maximum inner-product retrieval can be implemented with approximate nearest-neighbor search. At runtime, when the verified token falls outside the current reduced vocabulary, the current draft hidden state is used as the query, and HNSW returns the top-NN semantic neighbors as the seed set.

Token co-occurrence graph.

The token co-occurrence graph is also built offline from tokenized SlimPajama using bigram-level statistics. An edge u→vu\rightarrow v is created whenever token vv immediately follows token uu, and edge weights are given by empirical conditional probabilities p⁡(v∣u)p(v\mid u). To keep the graph sparse and reproducible, we apply offline filtering with a minimum co-occurrence count of 5, a probability threshold τ=10−4\tau=10^{-4}, and a maximum out-degree of 64 per source token.

Runtime candidate formation.

At runtime, the initial candidate set is formed as the union of the target-side top-10 candidates at the rejection step and the HNSW top-10 semantic neighbors. For each token in this initial set, we further retrieve up to top-8 outgoing graph neighbors after pruning, merge all returned neighbors, and deduplicate them before insertion into the dynamic vocabulary.

ARC-based dynamic vocabulary maintenance.

To enforce a strict dynamic budget, we maintain the dynamic vocabulary using Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) with total capacity 256. ARC uses two main lists, T1T_{1} (recent) and T2T_{2} (frequent), together with two ghost lists, B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. In our implementation, the target parameter is initialized as p=128p=128 and constrained to [0,256][0,256], with |B1|=256|B_{1}|=256 and |B2|=256|B_{2}|=256. New tokens are first admitted to T1T_{1}; a second hit promotes them to T2T_{2}; and repeated hits in T2T_{2} move them to the MRU position. When the budget is exceeded, ARC evicts from T1T_{1} if |T1|>p|T_{1}|>p, and otherwise from T2T_{2}.

Additional safeguards.

For stability, we enable batch deduplication, cap the number of newly inserted tokens at 32 per failure event, require a minimum residency of 8 decoding steps before eviction, and keep the ARC target parameter fixed during the first 50 events as a warm-up phase. On the adaptation side, tokens inside the active vocabulary are only eligible for online alignment; actual replay-buffer insertion and LoRA optimization are further gated by genuine draft-target mismatch signals and buffer fullness. Therefore, the update cost should be interpreted as amortized overhead rather than a per-token optimization penalty.

Appendix B Universality Across Different Model Families

In Section 4.6, we demonstrated that EvoSpec generalizes to decoupled architectures (Vanilla SD) using the Qwen3 models. To further verify that our gains are not specific to a single model family or tokenizer distribution, we extend our evaluation to the Llama-3.2 series.

Setup. We replicate the decoupled Vanilla Speculative Decoding setting using Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct as the draft model and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as the target. This setup introduces a different vocabulary structure and training distribution compared to Qwen3. Furthermore, the 1B draft model represents a lower-capacity regime compared to the Qwen3-1.7B used in the main text, posing a stricter test for vocabulary alignment.

Results. Table 6 presents the results. We observe distinct behaviors compared to the main experiments:

  • •

    Projection Overhead in Lightweight Models: Unlike in larger models where static pruning often yields negligible gains, here the FR-Spec baseline achieves a noticeable speedup of 1.03×\times. We attribute this to the architectural characteristics of the 1B model, where the computational cost of the output projection layer constitutes a larger proportion of the total latency. Reducing the vocabulary size thus provides immediate arithmetic savings.

  • •

    Synergistic Acceleration with EvoSpec: Leveraging this inherent computational advantage, EvoSpec further amplifies the gains. By dynamically retrieving high-value tokens to restore acceptance rates, our method combines projection-layer efficiency with high prediction accuracy, pushing the speedup from 1.03×\times to 1.16×\times.

  • •

    Optimal Buffer Size: We observe that performance peaks at Dyna 256, suggesting that a compact dynamic buffer is sufficient to capture relevant context for this model scale. Increasing the buffer size further to 512 or 1024 introduces retrieval overheads that slightly outweigh the marginal gains in acceptance rate.

Appendix C Efficiency Analysis of Retrieval Latency and Masking

A primary concern with retrieval-augmented generation involves the potential latency overhead introduced by the retrieval process. In EvoSpec, we mitigate this challenge by offloading vocabulary retrieval tasks, including HNSW search and graph traversal, to the CPU for asynchronous execution. This design ensures that retrieval operations run in parallel with the GPU-bound speculative decoding steps.

To verify the efficacy of this asynchronous masking, we profiled the detailed execution timeline of a single speculative step. As illustrated in Figure 4, the CPU-based retrieval process is executed efficiently, completing in approximately 2.07 ms. In contrast, the concurrent GPU execution of the Transformer Body (before projection and sampling) requires 3.754 ms.

The retrieval is thus completed well before the decoding deadline, creating a safe margin of roughly 1.68 ms where the CPU waits for the GPU. Even accounting for the subsequent projection (lm_head, 0.561 ms) and sampling (0.025 ms) phases, the retrieval overhead is fully masked. This non-blocking design confirms that EvoSpec maintains optimal throughput by ensuring the GPU is effectively decoupled from CPU-side graph operations. Finally, it is worth noting that the HNSW index construction is performed only once offline, incurring no runtime overhead during the inference phase.

Appendix D Impact of Curriculum Decay Factor

The curriculum decay factor β\beta plays a pivotal role in governing the trade-off between filtering gradient noise and capturing long-range dependencies. A higher β\beta imposes a stricter penalty on uncertainty, effectively shortening the supervision horizon, whereas a lower β\beta approaches naive full-sequence optimization. To analyze its impact, we trained the draft model using β∈{0.0,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7}\beta\in\{0.0,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\} and plotted the validation loss dynamics.

As shown in Figure 5, the choice of β\beta significantly influences convergence quality. We observe three distinct behaviors:

  • •

    No Curriculum (β=0.0\beta=0.0): The model fails to converge effectively (gray dotted line), suffering from high variance caused by unreliable distal gradients. This confirms the necessity of our confidence-aware weighting mechanism.

  • •

    Optimal Balance (β=0.3\beta=0.3): The setting of β=0.3\beta=0.3 achieves the lowest loss (red solid line), indicating an optimal balance where the model filters out high-entropy noise while retaining sufficient signal for long-term alignment.

  • •

    Over-Correction (β>0.3\beta>0.3): Increasing β\beta to 0.50.5 or 0.70.7 results in suboptimal convergence. This suggests that overly aggressive decay suppresses valuable supervision signals from verified tokens, limiting the model’s ability to learn complex dependencies.

These results demonstrate that while EvoSpec outperforms the baseline, selecting an appropriate β\beta is critical for maximizing alignment efficiency.

Appendix E Qualitative Analysis: Dynamic Prefetching Mechanism

To illustrate how EvoSpec handles vocabulary limitations in specialized domains, we present a qualitative case study involving prostate cancer prognosis. Figure 6 visualizes the complete lifecycle of a dynamic retrieval event based on a real-world inference trace.

The process initiates at Time t0t_{0}, where the model encounters the term “nomograms”. The static draft model fails to predict the suffix “ograms” (identifying it as OOV), which immediately acts as a trigger for the semantic retrieval engine.

At Time t1t_{1}, utilizing the semantic context of the trigger, the system retrieves a cluster of high-probability domain terms, including “biochemical”, “recurrence”, and “PCS” (Prostate Cancer-Specific). These terms are actively pushed into the dynamic vocabulary buffer.

Finally, at Time t2t_{2}, the benefit of this retrieval is realized. After generating the intervening functional phrase “…designed to predict”, the draft model successfully hits the buffered terms to correctly generate the complex medical phrase “biochemical recurrence”. Crucially, this highlights the semantic prefetching effect: although retrieval is triggered reactively by the initial OOV event, the retrieved cluster covers the semantic neighborhood of the emerging topic. Consequently, the retrieval latency is incurred only once at the topic boundary, while subsequent domain-specific tokens are served instantly from the dynamic buffer, effectively amortizing the initial cost over the entire conversation segment.

Appendix F Direct Validation of Active-Vocabulary Coverage

The main paper motivates EvoSpec from a coverage perspective: the active vocabulary should retain as much target-model probability mass as possible while remaining compact enough for efficient draft-side projection. To directly validate this mechanism, we report the covered probability mass of the active vocabulary 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} under the default setting of Static 32k + Dynamic 256. For dynamic methods, we further report Recall@256 against the target model’s top-kk tokens. FR-Spec serves as the static baseline; Static 32k + HNSW isolates semantic retrieval; Static 32k + HNSW + Graph corresponds to the retrieval-stage result before online alignment; and EvoSpec is the full system.

These results directly validate the intended mechanism. Semantic retrieval substantially improves coverage over the static baseline, graph expansion provides a further consistent gain, and the full EvoSpec pipeline performs best. This trend is consistent with the view that online alignment not only improves draft-target consistency, but also modestly improves the quality of the hidden states used to query the dynamic shortlist.

Appendix G Long-Horizon Evaluation on Real Multi-Turn Traces

The main text evaluates dynamic distribution shifts using controlled topic-switching trajectories. To complement this controlled setting with a more realistic long-horizon test, we further evaluate EvoSpec on real multi-turn traces from LMSYS-Chat-1M. We use all 144 conversation trajectories containing more than 50 turns, and report the overall mean acceptance length (MAL) and end-to-end throughput over the full trajectory.

The results provide a stronger long-horizon robustness signal than synthetic topic-switching alone. EvoSpec remains superior over full real conversational traces in both acceptance length and end-to-end throughput, suggesting that its online adaptation mechanism does not collapse under naturally evolving user topics. While this evaluation is not a formal continual-learning benchmark, it offers a more deployment-relevant complement to the controlled switching analysis in the main paper.
